questions.question: Describe the military situation in the Pacific in 1945 and explain why Japan had not surrendered.
questions.expected_answer: The Allies island-hopped towards Japan (Nimitz, MacArthur); Iwo Jima (February-March 1945, about 21 000 Japanese and 6 800 Americans dead) and Okinawa (April-June, about 12 500 Americans, 110 000 Japanese soldiers and many civilians) were extremely costly, with kamikaze attacks. Firebombing (Tokyo, 9-10 March, about 100 000 dead) and blockade devastated Japan. Its leaders refused unconditional surrender because surrender was shameful, they feared for the emperor, hoped a costly final battle or Soviet mediation would bring better terms, and were divided.

questions.question: Describe the development and use of the atomic bombs in August 1945.
questions.expected_answer: The Manhattan Project (from 1942; Groves, Oppenheimer; about 130 000 workers, 2 billion dollars) built uranium and plutonium bombs; the Trinity test was on 16 July 1945. After the Potsdam Declaration (26 July) was rejected, the Enola Gay dropped Little Boy on Hiroshima at 8:15 on 6 August (about 140 000 dead by end of 1945, from blast, heat, fire and radiation). Fat Man was dropped from Bockscar on Nagasaki at 11:02 on 9 August (about 74 000 dead by end of 1945).

questions.question: Explain how World War II ended in the Pacific and why August 1945 began the nuclear age.
questions.expected_answer: The USSR declared war on 8 August and invaded Manchuria on 9 August, ending hopes of Soviet mediation. With the bombs, blockade and military collapse, Emperor Hirohito intervened; his surrender broadcast was on 15 August and Japan signed on the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945. The nuclear age began: the US monopoly ended when the USSR tested a bomb on 29 August 1949, starting an arms race (H-bombs 1952-53); survivors (hibakusha) and scientists campaigned for peace; nuclear power (Koeberg 1984); South Africa built and dismantled six bombs.
